item.title: Decoding BlackBuck’s Core Trucking Model And Its New Engines
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma

item.content:encoded:
A truck carrying goods across India spends several days or even weeks on the road, but it’s not just the vehicle that needs to keep moving. In fact, the technology watching and powering India’s trucking industry never stops, regardless of how slow or fast the journey is, or indeed whether it is the slow sales months or the peak festive season. 

It is this technology that has made life easier over the years, for those reliant on India’s trucking system for delivery of parcels and goods. The transformation seen in the past decade has lifted businesses and startups in retail, ecommerce and logistics sectors.  

The problem was manifold before technology changed things: Operators have to find loads for their vehicles, negotiate freight rates, make toll payments, track fuel consumption, monitor fleets and arrange financing. For an industry as fragmented as India’s trucking market, these everyday tasks can add to the cost and complexity of running a fleet.

It was this problem that BlackBuck set out to address when it was founded in 2015. The company began as a marketplace connecting truck operators with businesses looking to transport goods. Over the years, it expanded beyond load discovery to build a wider digital platform for truck operators, bringing payments, fleet tracking, freight services and vehicle financing under one umbrella.

Today, its offerings span five business lines — payments, telematics, loads classifieds, superloads and vehicle financing. While payments and telematics form its core businesses, the other three are classified as growth businesses.

What The Q2 Numbers Show

The expansion has translated into higher revenue. In Q2 FY27, BlackBuck reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹235.33 Cr, up 55.7% YoY from ₹151.14 Cr. Its net profit rose 41.8% to ₹41.4 Cr from ₹29.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Total income, including other income, increased 51.4% to ₹253.15 Cr.

But the growth is not coming from its established businesses alone. Revenue from its core Payments and Telematics businesses grew 31% to ₹161.39 Cr, while its growth businesses grew 166% to ₹73.94 Cr.

However, faster growth has its own cost.

Total expenses rose 64% YoY to ₹210.3 Cr during the quarter, with management attributing the increase primarily to customer acquisition across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads. Meanwhile, EBITDA stood at ₹50.61 Cr and adjusted EBITDA at ₹55.04 Cr.

During the Q2 earnings call, CEO Rajesh Yabaji said upfront acquisition costs can weigh on EBITDA even as the company expects to recover them over the lifetime of a customer. The company’s adjusted EBITDA grew at a slower 29% to ₹55.04 Cr.

“Wherever we see opportunities, we are expanding and gaining more market share. So, as and when there are spurts in customer acquisition, EBITDA suppresses in that particular quarter,” Yabaji said.

Clearly, there is a balancing act at the centre of BlackBuck’s business model. Its established businesses continue to generate operating cash flows, but the company is using that headroom to scale newer offerings. The question is whether these newer businesses can build sustainable economics without diluting the profitability of the core platform. To understand that, first, let’s decode how BlackBuck makes money.

BlackBuck’s Core: Monetising Trucking

While Payments and Telematics form its core businesses, BlackBuck has other verticals that contribute to its topline, including Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. These make up its newer businesses that leverage the core, and will play a role in BlackBuck’s future growth. But for now, the core is what sustains the trucking company. 

BlackBuck earns through commissions, subscriptions, service fees and interest income, depending on the service being offered. Its payments business is built around two major use cases — tolling and fuel purchases. Through its platform, truck operators can buy and manage FASTags, make toll payments and access fuel cards.

BlackBuck earns commissions from banks for distributing and managing FASTags and from oil marketing companies (OMCs) for fuel card distribution and management. It also collects service fees for FASTag issuance, replacement, activation and recharge transactions.

Meanwhile, the telematics segment takes the relationship beyond the toll booth. The business offers GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, fuel sensors and dashcams, with customers paying for devices and related services through subscriptions.

BlackBuck recognises this revenue over the contract period rather than booking the entire amount when a device is sold. This explains why strong device sales do not immediately translate into an equivalent jump in reported revenue.

Most of the revenue acceleration for Telematics device sales in the previous quarter came from state-level AIS mandates. Newer offerings such as fuel sensors and dashcams contributed a smaller share, with dashcams still being piloted. 

On The Periphery 

BlackBuck’s pitch is to become more than a platform that helps truck operators pay tolls. It wants to be part of several decisions they make while running their businesses.

It is built around getting a truck operator to return to the platform for more of the services needed to keep a truck running. The catch is that each additional service also brings its own costs, execution challenges, and pressure on the bottom line.

The aforementioned newer business segments take BlackBuck further into the freight and financing value chain. 

Loads Classifieds is a subscription-led marketplace where shippers post freight requirements and truck operators discover available loads. SuperLoads goes beyond listing loads. It offers managed freight services, matching shippers with truck operators and facilitating truck placements.

BlackBuck earns service income from these transactions, while truck hiring charges add to the cost of running the business.

Lastly, vehicle finance rounds out the offering by helping truck operators access loans to buy used commercial vehicles or raise finance against vehicles they already own. 

BlackBuck works mostly through lending partners, which managed around ₹600 Cr of assets on the platform at the time of its Q4 FY26 results, while its own book stood at roughly ₹60 Cr. It earns through fees and interest income.

It earns through fees and interest income associated with the financing activity. The lending business is claimed to be on track to achieve EBITDA break-even in FY27, supported by growth in assets under management on a relatively steady cost base.

The traction across these businesses is reflected in their combined performance. Revenue from BlackBuck’s growth businesses increased 266% to ₹126.51 Cr in FY26. In Q2 FY27, the combined revenue stood at ₹73.94 Cr, up 166% YoY.

What Goes Into Running The Truck Business

The expanding revenue portfolio also comes with a wider cost base. Running a payments platform and selling telematics subscriptions is one thing, but managing freight transactions and facilitating truck placements brings an additional layer of operational expenses.

The company has to spend on people, technology, customer acquisition and, in the case of SuperLoads, truck hiring as well.

Manpower services emerged as the largest named individual expense head at ₹153.3 Cr, compared with ₹118 Cr a year earlier. This was followed by truck hiring charges which is a new cost head for the company from FY26. 

The distinction between manpower services and employee benefits is worth noting. Employee benefits expense of ₹160.2 Cr covers the cost of BlackBuck’s employees, including salaries, bonuses, provident fund contributions, ESOP expenses, gratuity and staff welfare. 

Manpower services, reported separately under other expenses at ₹153.3 Cr, capture costs associated with outsourced and contract manpower.

Meanwhile, truck hiring charges are particularly interesting in the context of SuperLoads, one of the newer businesses the company has launched to bulk up its customer lifetime value. Unlike a classifieds platform that primarily monetises access to listings, a managed freight business has to coordinate truck availability and placements.

That creates a different cost equation. But BlackBuck does not disclose how much of the ₹74 Cr was specifically attributable to SuperLoads.

The pressure to invest to grow will continue till the end of FY27. During the Q2 earnings call, management said higher customer acquisition spending across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads contributed to the rise in expenses.

Management also pointed to improving productivity in SuperLoads’ older markets through AI-led matchmaking, which it believes can help improve unit economics as the business expands.

That is the bet BlackBuck is making: spend more to get truck operators and shippers onto the platform, then earn more from each customer through multiple services.

But customer acquisition only works as a growth lever if the additional transactions eventually generate enough revenue to cover the cost of acquiring and serving them. For now, the company is still building out that equation.

The Core Pays For The Growth

BlackBuck’s core businesses are still generating cash, but like many other listed tech companies these days, the company is choosing to reinvest a larger share of that headroom into customer acquisition and newer offerings. The idea is to boost the customer lifetime value and the engagement opportunities. 

This is beginning to show up in its operating leverage. CEO Yabaji said the core business historically delivered operating leverage of 70-85%, and at times 100%. In Q2 FY27, this had moderated to around 50% as the company stepped up upfront spending on acquiring customers.

“The nature of the core business continues to be a strong operating cash flow machine for the company. We are giving its due investments wherever needed, and we are seeing in a lot of niches a strong uptick in customer acquisition and revenue growth,” he added.

The lower operating leverage suggests that a larger share of the business’s earnings is being absorbed by the cost of acquiring customers and scaling newer offerings, rather than flowing through as incremental profit.

While the core continues to generate cash, its growth drivers are shifting. Telematics is gaining traction, but the tolling business has not seen a corresponding improvement in monetisation. BlackBuck’s next phase of growth rests on Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. While all three address different parts of the trucking value chain, they also represent a move beyond the company’s relatively established payments and telematics operations.

However, BlackBuck does not disclose revenue or profitability separately for Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. This makes it difficult to assess which business is driving the growth, how much each is costing to scale, or whether one is closer to profitability than the others.

For now, the numbers establish that these offerings are gaining traction. But growth alone will not determine whether they strengthen BlackBuck’s business model. The real test will be whether they can generate sustainable returns without relying indefinitely on the core.

item.title: Profits Are Just Half The Story This Earnings Season
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: The 2026 festive season began in muted fashion, but the performance of some of the key new-age tech stocks in…
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 festive season began in muted fashion, but the performance of some of the key new-age tech stocks in the pre-festive quarter (Q2 FY27) shows that even in this environment businesses are able to extract and expand profits, and grow their topline.

When we see the financial performance of ecommerce, fintech and logistics stocks, it’s clear companies entered this period with a lot more confidence and absorbed some of these headwinds. Pretty much each one of them improved on their profitability metrics and their topline. 

As Inc42 reported in October, early data from the festive season sales indicated that Indian consumers kept shopping, but with more abandon.

Online sales slipped from last year, card spending and smartphone sales weakened, and surveys suggest urban households are trimming discretionary budgets too. Rising household costs, uncertainty over jobs and incomes, and discounts that no longer feel compelling have made shoppers wary of big-ticket purchases. 

Consumers are still browsing for products, but in the current climate, conversion rates have fallen for premium products, which usually see a big uptick. 

A lot of this has to do with the macroeconomic factors, rising energy prices and logistics costs, and lingering grave geopolitical concerns that have dented consumer confidence and spending. 

In Q2, logistics tech players expanded capacity ahead of the festive shopping rush, with higher volumes offering an opportunity to improve operating leverage. Ecommerce companies capitalised on seasonal demand, even as the pressure to balance growth with profitability persisted. 

Meanwhile, fintech companies, particularly those with a big UPI focus, faced a different equation: the prospect of merchant discount rates (MDR) on select UPI transactions. While MDR itself is yet to come into effect, the fintech ecosystem’s quarter was defined by swelling toplines, which bodes well for the next quarter where MDR is likely to become a real factor. 

Profitability broadened across the listed new-age tech universe, with nine of the 11 large tech stocks (with a market cap of over ₹10,000 Cr) across these key sectors reporting a net profit in Q2 FY27. 

The combined bottomline of these companies improved by around ₹1,100–1,400 Cr year-on-year (YoY), depending on how exceptional items in the base quarter are treated, according to market data. 

More importantly, EBITDA grew faster than revenue at all nine profitable companies, suggesting that operating leverage is beginning to show up in reported performance.

But a significant profit pool remained concentrated in a handful of companies, while businesses such as Swiggy and Meesho continue to report losses despite improving operating metrics. 

Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the market is moving towards rewarding earnings delivery rather than growth narratives. “Over the next 12–18 months, we expect earnings delivery, rather than growth narratives, to be the main driver of returns in this space,” he said,

This distinction is particularly relevant when the three major segments, fintech, logistics and ecommerce are assessed separately. 

Fintech has delivered the strongest operating performance, logistics has shown some of the clearest margin improvement, and ecommerce has produced a wide range of outcomes. But how did the profitability story unfolded across these three sectors?

Logistics Tech Shifts Into High Gear

It was largely a capacity-building quarter for logistics companies, with the full benefit of festive demand expected to play out in Q3. Yet, the results already point to improving operating leverage, as shipment volumes grew faster than revenue at the larger third-party logistics (3PL) players.

Shadowfax’s revenue rose 57%, while express and hyperlocal orders grew nearly 70%. Adjusted EBITDA increased sharply, with margins expanding to 5%. Delhivery reported a similar divergence: express shipments grew 32%, against 22% growth in express revenue. Its adjusted EBITDA margin also improved, while first-half operating cash flow more than doubled.

The gap between volume and revenue growth suggests that incremental shipments are not translating into proportionate revenue. Profitability, therefore, will depend on whether higher volumes can offset pricing pressure and rising costs across fuel, wages and last-mile delivery.

Delhivery’s return to profitability also needs context: the year-ago quarter included acquisition-related integration costs linked to Ecom Express. Its adjusted EBITDA and cash generation offer a more useful measure of underlying progress.

Shiprocket, meanwhile, turned profitable, reporting a net profit of ₹60 Lakh against a loss of ₹20.3 Cr a year ago. Revenue grew 35%, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled. Its core business continued to expand, with transactions growing 31% and adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 12.8%. The results point to improving economics, although the reported profit remains modest.

Across the sector, technology and network utilisation are central to the margin story. 

Shadowfax is deploying AI-led route optimisation and expanding its seller platform, while Delhivery is investing in automation and autonomous material-handling systems. These initiatives could improve productivity, but their returns will depend on execution and the ability to absorb peak-season volumes without adding costs at the same pace.

The festive quarter will be the real test. Stronger volumes should support operating leverage, but sustained margin expansion will require better network utilisation, disciplined pricing and control over fulfilment costs. Logistics is showing clearer signs of improving economics, though the gap between shipment growth and revenue realisation remains a key risk.

Fintech’s Profit Engines Roar

Fintech was the strongest performer in Q2 FY27, with all the major companies in the segment reporting profits. Moreover, EBITDA growth outpaced revenue growth at each, pointing to improving operating leverage. The gains, however, are coming from deeper monetisation of existing customers rather than payment volumes alone.

Paytm is increasingly diversifying beyond payments, with financial services distribution contributing about a third of its revenue. Its merchant subscription base and financial services business continue to expand, reducing its dependence on payment processing.

Meanwhile, Pine Labs is extracting more value from its merchant network through subscriptions, affordability products and transaction-linked services. PB Fintech’s growing renewal book offers a similar advantage: recurring insurance revenue is expanding faster than its core insurance business, making growth less dependent on fresh policy acquisition. 

The bigger question for fintech is whether these operating gains can withstand regulatory changes. The proposed UPI MDR framework could create an additional revenue stream, but the benefit to payment companies will depend on how the pool is shared between banks and other ecosystem participants. With implementation postponed beyond the festive period, it remains an opportunity rather than an earnings driver for now.

Insurance distribution faces a more direct overhang. The proposed changes to commission structures and expense limits could alter the economics of online intermediaries such as PB Fintech. Its growing renewal revenue offers some cushion, but the impact on new-policy distribution remains uncertain.

“While fintech companies have demonstrated an ability to improve monetisation and operating leverage, the regulatory environment remains a key determinant of how sustainable these gains will be. For this segment, regulation is a bigger variable than execution,” said Thakkar.

Ecommerce’s Profitability Divide Widens

Ecommerce delivered the widest divergence in Q2 FY27. While revenue growth remained strong across quick commerce, ecommerce and consumer brands, profitability varied sharply, reflecting differences in scale, cost structures and monetisation. 

For example, Meesho saw its net loss narrow to 68%, while marketplace contribution margin improved to 6% of NMV from 3.3% a year ago. However, newer initiatives remain loss-making and are yet to establish meaningful scale.

Consumer brands delivered a more consistent earnings performance. Nykaa’s profit more than tripled, supported by margin expansion and growth across beauty and fashion. Lenskart also reported strong profit growth, with expansion across its India and international businesses. Higher store productivity, rising volumes and operating cash flow suggest that growth is being supported by better utilisation of the existing network, alongside store additions.

Input-cost inflation remains another pressure point for consumer brands. Passing on higher costs through pricing could protect margins but risks weighing on demand and average order values. Gross margins, customer retention and acquisition costs will be as important as revenue growth in assessing the durability of earnings.

Why Profits Are Just Half The Story

As these sectors continue to mature, operating leverage is becoming more important than headline growth. However, profitability remains concentrated, with a handful of companies accounting for a substantial share of the sector’s earnings. 

The ownership shift is also worth watching. 

Foreign investors have reduced exposure to several listed new-age tech companies, while domestic institutions have increased participation. But domestic ownership is no guarantee against corrections when earnings or regulatory developments disappoint.

According to market analysts, retail investors are likely to increasingly favour companies that are not only profitable but also generate revenue from multiple products within their existing customer base and use operating cash flow to fund expansion. 

We can see this in the aggressive diversification across the industry, particularly in fintech and logistics tech. 

This wave favours established fintech businesses, asset-light logistics networks and ecommerce companies where the seller-customer flywheel is up and running. 

Post the festive season spike, even if it may be a relatively smaller spike compared to previous years, the cash generation and regulatory resilience of these companies will be worth watching. That could very well mark the next phase of maturity.  

MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE

Inside Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO: As Razorpay gears up for its ₹6,000 Cr IPO, the proposed UPI merchant discount rate and its AI ambitions could shape its valuation. But can these growth levers convince public market investors to look beyond its thin margins?

Honasa’s Profit Up 87%: The Mamaearth parent reported an 87% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹73.2 Cr, while revenue rose 36% to ₹731.2 Cr. Growth across focus categories, offline channels and younger brands helped drive the company’s quarterly performance.

Go Digit PAT Dips: Go Digit’s net profit declined 31.1% YoY to ₹142.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 despite a marginal 1.7% rise in insurance revenue to ₹2,720.5 Cr. Higher insurance service expenses and claims weighed on profitability, even as motor insurance revenue grew.

RateGain Profit Rises 47%:The travel-focused SaaS company’s profit rose 46.5% YoY to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by operating revenue zooming 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr. This came on the back of the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn last year.

Moneyview Revenue Grows 41%: The fintech company’s consolidated net profit surged 417.6% YoY to ₹200.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 41% to ₹1,120.2 Cr. The fintech reported a managed AUM of ₹23,892 Cr, with its shares gaining 5.7% following the earnings announcement.

[Edited by Shishir Parasher]

item.title: Pronto’s Second Shift
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable…
item.content:encoded:
Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals. 

Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit. 

This is being built in Silicon Valley.

Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots. 

The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified. 

In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits.

In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models. 

A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. 

Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. 

Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all. 

The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment.

The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems?

Why Record Workers?

The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals. 

To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device.

“The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42.

Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims. 

What’s the point of all this?

Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected.

This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities.

The Missing Data Layer

One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions. 

The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process.

Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI. 

India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies. 

But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments.

Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments. 

Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape.

For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models. 

Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material.

Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited.

He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said.

Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties. 

Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US.

Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal.  

Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network.

The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier. 

More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature.

The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months. 

While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures. 

At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them. 

Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape. 

For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised. 

The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers? 

Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them.

Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity.

Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners.

An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose.

Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data. 

India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear. 

For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform.

The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto. 

Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.

[Edited by Nikhil Subramaniam]

item.title: New-Age Tech Stocks Extend Rally, CarTrade Leads With 23.3% Gain
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, with 54 of the 69 companies under Inc42’s coverage posting gains ranging…
item.content:encoded:
New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, with 54 of the 69 companies under Inc42’s coverage posting gains ranging from 0.4% to 23.3%.

CarTrade led the gainers, rebounding 23.3% after last week’s steep decline to close at ₹2,699.30. Awfis followed with a 20.4% rise to ₹281.65, while ixigo climbed 19.1%.

Recently listed Tonbo Imaging and Zetwerk touched fresh highs during the week. Lenskart, Ather Energy, Eternal, and Nykaa were also among the stocks that hit 52-week highs.

The gains lifted the combined market capitalisation of the 69 companies to $169.3 Bn from $160.9 Bn last week, an increase of 5.2%.

Among the losers, RateGain fell the highest by 9.19% to close the week at ₹725.90.

Here are some key developments from listed new-age tech companies during the week: 

Kissht’s AUM Crosses ₹10,000 Cr: Kissht’s assets under management (AUM) crossed ₹10,000 Cr, driven by growth in personal loans and its expansion into loans against property. The company attributed the growth to its AI-led underwriting and digital collections infrastructure, adding that its recent ₹832.2 Cr preferential issue strengthened its capital base.

MobiKwik Secures NBFC Licence: MobiKwik received an RBI licence to operate as an NBFC, following in-principle approval in April 2026. It plans to begin operations within three to six months and disburse ₹5,000 Cr in consumer and MSME loans over three to four years through an asset-light co-lending model.

Pine Labs Partners With Stripe: Pine Labs partnered with Stripe to offer Singapore retailers a unified platform for online and in-store payments, combining Stripe’s online infrastructure with Pine Labs’ terminals and merchant tools. The companies plan to expand the offering to other Southeast Asian markets in 2027. Pine Labs served 11.6 Lakh merchants across more than 22 markets at the end of Q2 FY27.



Here’s a look at the performance of the broader markets this week.

Benchmarks Jump Over 8%

Indian equities recorded a sharp weekly recovery, with the Nifty 50 gaining 8.6%, or 1,977 points, to close at 25,030.35. The Sensex rose 8.8%, or 6,568 points, to 81,028.02. Both benchmarks advanced in all five sessions, with the Nifty ending at its weekly high.

The broader market’s gains were smaller, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 rising 5.8% and 2.8%, respectively.

Renewed foreign investor buying, strong Q2 FY27 earnings, easing geopolitical concerns, and lower crude oil prices supported sentiment. Lower bond yields and a softer dollar also helped.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought a net ₹45,960 Cr of equities across the five sessions, marking their second consecutive week of buying after a 10-week selling streak. The inflows exceeded the ₹45,162 Cr they sold during October.

Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) sold a net ₹24,197 Cr, ending an 11-week buying streak. Together, the two investor groups remained net buyers of approximately ₹21,763 Cr.

Geojit Investments’ head of research Vinod Nair attributed the improved sentiment to strong Q2 earnings, healthy October auto sales, and firm GST collections, alongside easing concerns around the Iran conflict and tariffs following the US midterm election verdict.

He also pointed to foreign investors rotating out of crowded AI trades. The Indian market’s rally coincided with a selloff in global AI and semiconductor stocks.

Private banks led the gains following renewed foreign investor interest in a segment previously weighed down by concerns over net interest margins. Automobile and consumption stocks benefited from festive demand, while IT and PSU banks recorded relatively modest gains.

The sustainability of foreign inflows, crude oil prices, and developments in West Asia will remain key market triggers. Remaining Q2 results, US inflation and jobs data, and India’s inflation print will also influence trading.

Nair cautioned that intermittent profit booking could follow the sharp gains, although the near-term outlook remains constructive. He favours large-cap companies with earnings visibility and a buy-on-dips approach.

Meanwhile, the stock market will open for a special Muhurat trading session tomorrow, from 14:20 IST to 15:30 IST, on the occasion of Diwali. 

Now, let’s take a detailed look at the performance of Awifs and RateGain this week.

Awfis Rallies After Q2 Results

Awfis shares gained 20.4% this week to close at ₹281.65, following a near-doubling of its consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27. Net profit rose 92.8% to ₹30.8 Cr from ₹16 Cr a year ago and increased 28.5% from ₹24 Cr in the preceding quarter.

Operating revenue grew 19.6% YoY and 3.2% QoQ to ₹438.7 Cr. Awfis reported normalised revenue of ₹451 Cr, including an adjustment of around ₹13 Cr for actual rent received under finance lease arrangements. On this basis, coworking and allied services contributed approximately ₹376 Cr, while construction and fit-out projects under its Transform vertical generated ₹75 Cr.

Awfis added six centres during the quarter, taking its network to 254 centres with approximately 1.74 Lakh seats across 18 cities. Portfolio occupancy stood at 76.2%, rising to 84.1% at centres operational for more than 12 months.

Its premium portfolio comprised 29 Gold and 10 Elite centres. The company said incremental premium seats were being signed at prices around 35% higher than its flagship offerings.

Awfis plans to prioritise occupancy, client renewals, and capital-efficient expansion, while adding premium workspaces in Pune, Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi NCR.

RateGain Falls Despite Growth

RateGain shares declined 9.2% this week to close at ₹725.90, despite reporting a 46.5% YoY increase in consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27. The company’s stock plunged by over 11% on Friday, the next trading session after its quarterly disclosures. 

Operating revenue surged 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, largely reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, acquired for $250 Mn in November 2025.

Sequentially, however, revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr, while net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr.

Excluding expenses related to deferred deal consideration for Sojern, adjusted net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr.

The acquisition has reshaped RateGain’s business mix. Marketing technology accounted for 80.2% of revenue, followed by data-as-a-service at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%.

Its customer base stood at 14,538 at September-end, around 4.5 times the 3,224 customers reported at the end of FY25. Customers include hotel chains, online travel agencies, airlines, car rental companies, and destination marketing organisations.

RateGain’s UK subsidiary repaid another $46.3 Mn of acquisition-related debt during the quarter. Cumulative repayments reached $93.8 Mn, or 75% of the original $125 Mn facility from HSBC and Citibank, leaving outstanding debt of $31.3 Mn.

The company reported a sales pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said its second-half priorities included expanding the combined RateGain-Sojern offering and increasing customer adoption of its AI products.

item.title: OYO Parent PRISM’s Profit Jumps 17% YoY To ₹353 Cr In Q1
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: IPO-bound hospitality chain PRISM, the parent entity of OYO, reported a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹353 Cr in…
item.content:encoded:
IPO-bound hospitality chain PRISM, the parent entity of OYO, reported a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹353 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 17.3% from ₹301 Cr in the year-ago period.

According to PRISM’s audited financials seen by Inc42, the profitability came largely on the back of a deferred tax credit of nearly ₹244 Cr in the quarter under review. 

Nevertheless, PRISM continued to grow its top line and generated an operating revenue of ₹2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27. This was nearly 35% higher than ₹2,078 Cr reported in the year ago quarter.

The IPO-bound startup also managed to improve its EBITDA by 24.3% to ₹760 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹611 Cr in Q1 FY26. On the operational front, PRISM’s gross booking value (GBV) stood at nearly ₹9,600 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, up nearly 30% from ₹7,408 Cr in Q1 FY26. 

This is largely in line with what PRISM founder and CEO Ritesh Agarwal had said during the company’s extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in October this year.

“Our performance (in Q1 FY27) across segments on hotels or on vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins, higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand,” Agarwal had said then.

During the EGM, Agarwal also attributed PRISM’s performance to investments made in technology, brands and distribution capabilities over the past few years.

Founded in 2012 by Agarwal, OYO initially operated a budget hotel chain. It has since grown into a hospitality giant that offers holiday homes, coworking spaces, motels and corporate stays in more than 35 countries. The startup’s parent Oravel Stays rebranded to PRISM last year ahead of its initial public offering (IPO).

The startup has raised about $3.5 Bn in funding to date and counts the likes of SoftBank, Lightspeed India, Peak XV Partners and Microsoft among its backers.

The Q1 FY27 performance comes as PRISM is gearing up to list on the bourses. The hospitality giant first filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in December last year.

It then received the market regulator’s approval for its IPO in June this year. Right after, the startup filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. 

The Ritesh Agarwal-led startup is said to be eyeing a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn for the public issue.

item.title: ED Searches CoinDCX & Delta Exchange Over Alleged Illegal Cross-Border Transfers
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) conducted searches at three premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI)…
item.content:encoded:
The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) conducted searches at three premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks. 

In a statement, the agency said the searches were conducted between November 4 and November 5 across Bengaluru. The crypto trading transactions in question run into thousands of crores of Rupees, as per ED.

“ED Bengaluru has conducted search(es) at three premises linked to Neblio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (CoinDCX parent) and Excelium Technologies Pvt. Ltd.(which operates Delta Exchange India) under FEMA 1999 in the case of large scale unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto token derivatives and real world asset tokens,” said ED in a statement.

As per the directorate, ED began its probe into the matter after receiving information of alleged forex violations by CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India.

The agency alleged that CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India facilitated spot trading, futures and options (F&O) trading and trading in tokenised shares of foreign companies – all through cryptocurrencies. 

ED also claimed CoinDCX advertised these products despite not being authorised to offer them.

While CoinDCX is yet to issue a statement on the matter, Delta Exchange India said that it cooperated “fully” with the officials and furnished the information sought. In a post on X, the crypto exchange further claimed that it is not involved in “any cross-border transfer of VDAs (virtual digital assets) in any form or manner”.

“We acknowledge the Enforcement Directorate’s statement regarding their visit to our premises on 4th & 5th November… We cooperated fully with the officials and provided the information that they sought. We remain committed to extending our support and cooperation as may be required…,” said Delta Exchange India. 

CoinDCX’s Alleged Modus Operandi

According to the ED, user funds (deposited in Rupees) were allegedly converted into stablecoins, primarily USDT, and then transferred to overseas crypto platforms including Binance, KuCoin, Gate.io and Bybit. The agency alleged that these transfers circumvented forex rules governing cross-border money transfers.

For spot trades, the ED alleged that CoinDCX used an account, opened in the name of a Costa Rica-based entity, to send the USDT to foreign crypto platforms. Describing the Costa Rican company as a mere “paper entity”, the agency alleged that the transactions were allegedly actually executed directly through CoinDCX APIs.

The directorate also made similar allegations for CoinDCX’s F&O product. ED said that the homegrown platform allegedly opened matching positions via APIs on foreign platforms after users placed orders, with settlements occurring overseas when positions were closed.

The ED also claimed that tokenised-stock trading on CoinDCX was routed through Hyperliquid, an overseas decentralised crypto trading platform. It said that user funds were converted into USDT to open positions, with settlements completed on the overseas platform.

The alleged volumes of spot, derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions were described as running into thousands of crores of rupees. The ED also alleged that CoinDCX paid hundreds of crores in transaction fees to foreign platforms in stablecoins. This, the agency said, contravened forex rules.

Delta Exchange India Under ED Radar

Just like CoinDCX, the Directorate of Enforcement also alleged that Delta Exchange India offered spot trading, crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks via cryptocurrencies. 

It alleged that a large volume of DEI’s derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions was routed through CoinDCX, which in turn executed them on foreign platforms. 

The agency alleged that Delta Exchange India also transferred hundreds of crores of Rupees to overseas associate entities. These transfers are under investigation, added the ED.

In a statement, the ED said the fintech products offered by both crypto exchanges appear to have prima facie contravened norms under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The investigation remains ongoing. 

The searches are part of ED’s broader clampdown on forex violations involving crypto platforms. Just days ago, the directorate launched a probe into alleged FEMA violations involving crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform, Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr.

Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

item.title: Stockal’s US Trading Row: Missing Consent, A Chinese Microcap, And Unanswered Questions
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those…
item.script: var dlChartData = { json_key: 'Funding Amount Over Time', shortcode_key: 'Funding Amount Over Time', companyName: 'stockal', apiUrl: '/funding-amount/over-time/', maxyear: '2026', minyear: '2008', location: '', mindate: '', maxdate: '', rounds: '', industry: '', apiUrlsector: '', apiUrlLocation: '', investors: '', chartType: 'Area', donatType: '', financialType: '', timeframeType: '', }; // console.log('Global Variable dlChartData:', dlChartData);
item.content:encoded:
Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap.

Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares.

One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased.

Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions.

An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth.

How The Trades Unfolded

Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has raised over $15 Mn from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments.


Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile.

Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap.

Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials.

In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification.

An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account.

Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%.

Differing Accounts Of Access

In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions.

Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.” 

Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation.

Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far.

This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts.

Safeguards Under The Spotlight

The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades.

Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions.

He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication.

Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said.

Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear.

He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities.

Borderless Sets Out Its Position


Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts.

It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts.

The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators.

Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed.

Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response.

Who Bears The Responsibility?

The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024.

HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities.

While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses?

Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability.

For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established.

Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

item.title: MobiKwik To Begin NBFC Operations Within 6 Months Post RBI Clearance
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: MobiKwik’s wholly owned subsidiary, MobiKwik Financial Services Pvt Ltd (MFSPL), has received a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI…
item.content:encoded:
MobiKwik’s wholly owned subsidiary, MobiKwik Financial Services Pvt Ltd (MFSPL), has received a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI to operate as a non-banking financial company (NBFC).

The certificate was issued on November 5, following the RBI’s in-principle approval in April 2026. The dedicated NBFC was officially incorporated on March 13, 2025. 

With the regulatory clearance in place, MFSPL intends to commence operations over the next three to six months. It intends to operate on an asset-light co-lending model, partnering with banks and other NBFCs. 

In a statement, the company said that it plans to complement its existing lending service provider (LSP) business with the ability to originate credit directly through its NBFC. 

“This will provide greater flexibility in product development, faster go-to-market execution and opportunities to improve lending economics, while allowing the group to continue leveraging its partnerships with established lenders,” the company said.

MobiKwik aims to disburse loans worth ₹5,000 Cr over the next three to four years, covering secured and unsecured credit for consumers and MSMEs.

Cofounder and CFO Upasana Taku said that the NBFC extension would allow MobiKwik to build on its existing lender partnerships and technology infrastructure while participating more actively in the lending value chain. The company plans to focus on responsible lending, prudent underwriting and sustainable growth.

During its Q2 earnings call, the CFO noted that MobiKwik could initially route around 10% of its digital lending disbursals through the NBFC. If the company disburses ₹6,000 Cr through its digital lending business next year, it would aim to route ₹600 Cr through MFSPL.

Under a proposed 10:90 co-lending arrangement, MobiKwik would contribute 10% of the loan amount, while its lending partner would fund the remaining 90%. This would require around ₹60 Cr in capital from MobiKwik to support ₹600 Cr in disbursals, allowing it to limit its on-book exposure while leveraging its existing underwriting and collections capabilities.

The NBFC launch comes amid an uptick for MobiKwik’s business. MobiKwik reported a consolidated net profit of ₹11.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a net loss of ₹28.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. 

Operating revenue increased 9.4% YoY to ₹295.7 Cr from ₹270.2 Cr. The company said it recorded its highest-ever quarterly net profit, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter.

During the quarter, MobiKwik’s financial services business segment, which includes its ZIP EMI credit offering, increased 41.8% YoY to ₹86.9 Cr.

Loan disbursals through its lending partners rose 34.1% YoY to ₹1,082.6 Cr, up 46.9% sequentially from ₹736.7 Cr. The sequential recovery followed a temporary dip linked to technology infrastructure migration during the transfer of its lending business.

MobiKwik increased its major lending partners to 11 from six a year earlier. It classifies partners with quarterly disbursals exceeding ₹5 Cr as major lenders. Of the total disbursals, 21% came through its distribution model, while the remaining 79% were under its first-loss default guarantee (FLDG) model, under which it shares credit risk with lending partners.

Lending-related expenses, including operational and financial guarantee costs, declined 16.4% YoY to ₹29.8 Cr. The company attributed the reduction to improved credit quality and better commercial terms with lending partners.

MobiKwik expects lending disbursals to maintain strong double-digit growth as newer partnerships mature and it introduces additional product categories, although management cautioned that the growth rate may moderate.

Shares of MobiKwik ended today’s trading session 2.3% higher at ₹224.75 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Brokers In October: Angel One Climbs To The Second Spot With 2.4 Lakh New User Additions
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Indian stockbrokers’ combined total active user base shrunk by 0.5% to 4.59 Cr in October, dropping from 4.61 Cr users…
item.content:encoded:
Indian stockbrokers’ combined total active user base shrunk by 0.5% to 4.59 Cr in October, dropping from 4.61 Cr users in September. Despite the broader market plateau, user consolidation accelerated in favour of newer players. 

Groww continued to cement its market-leading position with 1.38 Cr active users in October, commanding a 30% market share. Notably, it added 3.04 Lakh users in the month, more than any other competitor in the top 10. 

To note, Groww’s net active client additions in October were approximately 1.5X the combined additions of the next four largest brokers by active client base, Angel One, Zerodha, ICICI Securities and Upstox, which collectively added around 2.02 lakh active clients. 

But the positions below saw an intriguing shakeup. 

Zerodha, after losing clients in many months over the past year, slipped from second place. 

Angel One overtook Zerodha, adding around 2.4 Lakh users to take its active user count to 69.99 Lakh and its market share to 15.3%. It grew at a 3.3% rate over the past month to overtake Zerodha. 

“During the quarter, Angel One acquired nearly 15 lakh new clients, up 11.6% from the previous quarter, taking its client base to 3.99 Cr by September before it crossed 4 Cr in October. Its wealth management business continued to scale, with assets under management rising 19.1% quarter-on-quarter and 160.5% year-on-year to ₹16,000 Cr,” the company said in a statement. 

Meanwhile, more than 32K users or around 0.5% of Zerodha’s active user base turned inactive over the previous month. It ended the month with 67.59 Lakh users, compared to 67.92 Lakh users in the previous month, although its market share remained nearly unchanged at 14.7%. 

ICICI Securities held its fourth place with 21.64 Lakh active users, adding 3.7 Lakh users in October to take its market share to 4.7% market share. 

In fifth place, Upstox shed 0.6% of its user base as the startup saw 11.3 Lakh users leave to bring its active user count down to 18.43 Lakh with a market share of just 4%. 

Kotak Securities occupied sixth position with 14.05 Lakh active users while HDFC Securities finished seventh with 13.61 Lakh active users. The two bank-linked brokerages grew their user base by 0.9% and 0.5% respectively. 

Meanwhile, Dhan, in eighth place, added nearly 26K users over the past, as its user base increased 2.3% to 11.47 Lakh from 11.21 Lakh in September. It was able to match Groww in terms of growth rate to become the second fastest growing brokerage among the top 10 after Angel One. 

SBI Securities lost the most users after Zerodha, with an exodus of 17K users or 1.7% of its user base. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets saw its active user count decline to 10.04 Lakh compared to 10.21 Lakh in September. 

Rounding off the top 10, Motilal Oswal’s active user count grew 0.8% to 9.16 Lakh from 9.09 Lakh.

Beyond the top 10, Sahi added 34,372 active clients during October, adding to its bid to solidify its name in the discount brokerage space. 

Markets Recover In The Month Of October

October marked a modest recovery for Indian equities after September’s sharp correction, although foreign investor selling remained elevated. The Nifty 50 rose 2.81% while Sensex gained over 3%. The gains ended the benchmarks’ two-month losing streak, but the recovery was not broad-based, with mid- and small-cap stocks continuing to face pressure. 

As per data shared by Bajaj Broking, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were net sellers of ₹45,162 Cr in October, while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) bought shares worth ₹62,220 Cr on a net basis. However, foreign selling eased in the second half of the month, with FPIs turning net buyers and investing ₹13,112 Cr between October 16 and 31, after pulling out nearly ₹47,955 Cr in the first fortnight.

“Going ahead, the reversal in FII flows is an encouraging signal for sentiment, though elevated crude and global event risk could temper the momentum,” Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking had noted.

item.title: AvenuesAI Q2 Net Profit Rises 6% YoY To ₹72 Cr, Revenue Up 47%
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September…
item.content:encoded:
AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.7 Cr a year earlier. On a sequential basis, net profit declined 15.4% from ₹84.8 Cr.

Meanwhile, its operating revenue grew 46.5% YoY and 7.4% QoQ to ₹287.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Including other income of ₹2.8 Cr, total income during the quarter stood at ₹290.7 Cr. 

The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% YoY to ₹9.9 Cr. This came as its total expenses rose 49.4% YoY and 7.7% QoQ to ₹282.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, outpacing the growth in operating revenue.

At the same time, its consolidated net revenue, after accounting for payment processing and other costs, declined 1% YoY to ₹151.3 Cr in Q2 FY27. 

AvenuesAI attributed the decline to its ‘competitive pricing strategy’ amid efforts to deepen merchant relationships and increase transaction volumes. As a result, its net take rate moderated 4% to 5.06 bps despite a 19% sequential increase in its total payments volume to ₹1.77 Lakh Cr. 

The company generated ₹282.2 Cr in revenue from its payment business, which includes its CCAvenue payment gateway, payment infrastructure services to banks (CPGS), and credit and lending-related services, accounting for nearly 98% of its operating revenue during the quarter. The remaining ₹5.7 Cr was derived from its ecommerce platform business, Rediff. 

AvenuesAI Looks To Unlock Value Across Subsidiaries

Alongside its financial performance, AvenuesAI outlined its plans to expand its AI capabilities, with advanced technology development and AI software-related work remaining among the key objectives of its rights issue. 

In June last year, the company had raised ₹700 Cr via a rights issue, primarily for the repayment of outstanding loans, expansion of its IPO-bound digital content and ecommerce marketplace Rediff and further investments in its AI arm, Nueromind, for which it had earmarked ₹294 Cr. 

Almost 42.7%, or ₹297.2 Cr, of the net proceeds remained unutilised at the end of the September quarter.

AvenuesAI has now announced that it will directly utilise the funds for AI development and software-related activities instead of routing the investment through Nueromind. It clarified that the change was limited to the mode of implementation, with no alteration to the end use of the proceeds.

In the June quarter, AvenuesAI announced plans to amalgamate Nueromind with itself, subject to NCLT approval.

It is also developing its Transaction Intelligence Score (TISco), an AI-led initiative that will use permitted transaction and merchant-behaviour signals for risk assessment, fraud prevention, merchant intelligence and financial services workflows.

The company aims to use its transaction infrastructure to build an intelligence layer that can support merchant and enterprise services.

On the investment front, AvenuesAI said it made investments in two financial services companies during the September quarter. It acquired a stake of up to 7% in Online PSB Loans Limited for a consideration of up to ₹65 Cr. It also invested up to ₹34.5 Cr to acquire a stake of up to 1.38% in Ratnaafin Capital Private Limited.

The company also reiterated its plans to expand CCAvenue’s international payments business, particularly in the US, by leveraging its payment technology, enterprise relationships and regulated infrastructure.

Meanwhile, its ecommerce arm, Rediff, is on its way to the bourses for a separate listing. After filing for an IPO confidentially earlier this year, the markets regulator SEBI approved the draft papers in August. 

However, the Q2 disclosure did not provide an update on Rediff’s proposed IPO. As per sources, Rediff would look to raise in between ₹600-800 Cr via the IPO

AvenuesAI outlined that unlocking value from Rediff is one of its three strategic priorities for FY27. It plans to integrate Rediff’s consumer and enterprise digital ecosystem with its payments and AI capabilities. This includes RediffOne, which offers digital commerce and communication services, and RediffPay, which is intended to expand consumer payment engagement.

AvenuesAI has maintained its FY27 consolidated revenue guidance of ₹1,100-1,300 Cr.

The company said its focus for the remainder of FY27 will remain on expanding merchant relationships, improving operating discipline and creating additional monetisation opportunities through Rediff, enterprise technology and applied AI.

It is also monitoring potential changes to the merchant discount rate (MDR) policy for eligible UPI transactions, with any introduction, timing or scope remaining subject to government and regulatory decisions.

Shares of AvenueAI ended today’s trading session 3.72% lower at ₹129.25.

item.title: MakeMyTrip Acquires Majority Stake In Quick Ride To Enter Ride Pooling
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick…
item.content:encoded:
Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride for an undisclosed amount.

In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.”

As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited, in which MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business.

However, Quick Ride’s erstwhile electric vehicle (EV) taxi business will remain with its predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Pvt Ltd.

Founded in 2014 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride offers a ride-sharing application that connects passengers to riders. It connects the commuters travelling in the same direction.

It also offers an enterprise solution for shared mobility and counts IT companies such as Wipro, TCS, Infosys, IBM and Cognizant, among others as its clients. Its services are available in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kochi, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, and Kolkata.

The startup has raised over $14 Mn from investors like Sequoia, Prosus and Venture Highway. Sequoia exited the startup in 2021. 

MakeMyTrip’s Acquisition-Led Expansion

The Quick Ride acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip’s broader strategy to expand its presence across adjacent travel and mobility segments through strategic investments and acquisitions.

Commenting on the acquisition, MakeMyTrip group CEO Rajesh Magow said that the investment would help the company establish a presence in daily intra-city commutes while strengthening its intercity travel offerings.

“As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel,” he added.

The company plans to leverage its experience in building redBus across India and overseas markets to scale Quick Ride’s ride-pooling business.

In the past few years, MakeMyTrip has acquired Savaari to strengthen its car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys.

The development comes as MakeMyTrip looks to deepen its presence across the travel value chain, moving beyond conventional travel bookings towards a broader set of transportation and ancillary services.

On the financial front, the travel tech major’s consolidated net profit for the three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) plunged 65% to $9.1 Mn from $25.8 Mn in the year-ago period. MakeMyTrip’s revenue grew 6% YoY to $285.6 Mn.
