item.title: Delhi HC Upholds BharatPe’s Veto Rights In Unity SFB Shareholding Dispute
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Adding another layer to the ongoing shareholder dispute at BharatPe-backed Unity Small Finance Bank (SFB), the Delhi High Court (HC)…
item.content:encoded:
Adding another layer to the ongoing shareholder dispute at BharatPe-backed Unity Small Finance Bank (SFB), the Delhi High Court (HC) has rejected an appeal filed by the bank against an interim order.

The interim order restrains Unity SFB from placing a proposed capital restructuring resolution before its board without prior written consent from BharatPe parent Resilient Innovations (RIPL) and Centrum Financial Services.

The order, passed by a bench Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar on November 5, restrains  Unity SFB from tabling, discussing or approving ‘Agenda Item 18’ at its board meeting without prior written consent from RIPL and Centrum Financial Services. The HC granted BharatPe the interim relief pertaining to the case earlier this year in July

The dispute stems from a Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) signed between Unity Bank, RIPL and Centrum in October 2021, following their partnership to establish Unity SFB. 

The agreement features certain ‘Reserved Matters’ that would require prior written consent from representatives of both RIPL and Centrum. These include changes to the bank’s capital structure and amendments to its constitutional documents.

Agenda Item 18 proposed increasing Unity SFB’s authorised share capital from ₹4,000 Cr to ₹4,900 Cr by creating an additional 90 Cr preference shares of ₹10 each. The proposal also involved amending the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MoA) to facilitate the issuance of these shares.

RIPL opposed the proposal, arguing that the proposed capital restructuring could dilute its shareholding in Unity SFB from 49% to 21%. It contended that the resolution fell under the SHA’s Reserved Matters and therefore required prior written consent from both RIPL and Centrum.

Welcoming the decision, BharatPe said the ruling reaffirmed the shareholder rights and governance framework agreed upon when the joint venture was established in 2021.

“The board must ensure that the bank complies with the court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders,” a BharatPe spokesperson said.

The company also called on Unity’s board to respect the governance processes agreed upon at the time of the bank’s inception and honour its contractual obligations under the SHA. It said the agreed framework should not be set aside to favour one shareholder group over another.

Unity Small Bank, on the other hand, declined to comment on the matter.

“The discussions are solely between the bank’s promoter and a financial investor. The bank remains operationally unaffected, and continues to serve its customers and stakeholders as usual,” the bank told Inc42.

The proposal also involved amending Clause V of the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MOA) to reflect the revised authorised capital.

While the bank acknowledged in its board agenda that the proposed capital increase was a ‘Reserved Matter’ under the SHA and sought RIPL and Centrum’s approval, it also proposed taking the resolution up for board discussion and approval.

RIPL opposed the move, arguing that a clause of the SHA expressly prohibits even discussing a Reserved Matter at a board meeting without prior written consent from both shareholders. It also relied on Clause 8, which bars the bank from taking decisions or actions on Reserved Matters without the requisite consent.

On the financial front, Unity SFB has seen significant growth since commencing operations in November 2021. In Q4 FY25, its operating revenue surged 123% YoY to ₹977 Cr, while net profit increased 83% to ₹264 Cr. For the full FY25, the bank reported revenue of ₹2,837 Cr and net profit of ₹482 Cr.

Notably, the financial results for FY26 are yet to be disclosed. On the other hand, BharatPe’s FY26 operating revenue increased by 11% YoY to ₹1,862 Cr, adjusted EBITDA profit rose 20% to ₹146 Cr as per a report by ANI. The company is yet to file its annual report for the fiscal.

Meanwhile, BharatPe’s parent RIPL, which holds a 49% stake in Unity SFB, was reportedly exploring a stake sale in January 2025. The company was looking to offload up to 25% of its stake in the bank to raise around $800 Mn.

The proposed sale was also linked to regulatory requirements mandating BharatPe to bring down its shareholding in the bank to 10% within eight years of its commencement of operations, by 2029. The company is yet to pare its stake.

item.title: MDR And AI: Inside The Two Acronyms That Could Shape Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO
item.dc:creator: Bismah Malik
item.description: In March this year, on the sidelines of Razorpay’s annual flagship event FTX, CEO Harshil Mathur told Inc42 that what…
item.content:encoded:
In March this year, on the sidelines of Razorpay’s annual flagship event FTX, CEO Harshil Mathur told Inc42 that what mattered most to him was how Razorpay stands in the public markets, and not the fact that it went public.

Eight months on, that test now has a rough date as the company sets off on the last leg of its IPO journey. 

Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed IPO. The fintech major is looking to raise ₹5,000-6,000 Cr through a mix of fresh issue and offer for sale at a valuation of around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027. Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi are the reported bankers.

The headline number when it comes to Razorpay’s listing, or for that matter any listing within fintech circles, has been that of valuation.Sources suggest that Razorpay may be looking to list at a $5 Bn valuation, a markdown from the $7.5 Bn valuation that the company commanded in December 2021. 

But back in 2021, fintech valuations were sky high amidst a pandemic led funding boom that witnessed sharp corrections years down the line.

Another fintech major, PhonePe, paused its mega listing in March 2026, with reports suggesting that volatile geopolitical tensions and valuation concerns led the payments company to put its IPO plans on hold. It has since revived them on the back of MDR. Sources told Inc42 in September that PhonePe is targeting a listing between February and March 2027 at a valuation of about $10 Bn.

But Razorpay has a different story to tell the public investors as it seeks ₹5,000-6,000 Cr from them.

The first part of that story is profit. “When you take out that one-time cost of the reverse flip, Razorpay was profitable — that profitability streak is maintained throughout. We hope the financials will continue to improve from here as a company that’s continuously growing,” Mathur had told Inc42 earlier. 

In FY25, Razorpay slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs from moving its domicile to India. It did not disclose the size of the loss. The reverse flip tax bill has been reported at about ₹1,245 Cr, or about $150 Mn. A year earlier, in FY24, its payments business had reported a ₹34 Cr profit against a total revenue of ₹2,068 Cr or a net margin of 1.6%. 

The company claims to lead India’s digital payments processing market in terms of total payments volume and is expanding across Southeast Asia and other geographies, but monetising this scale has always been a problem when it comes to payments companies. 

The 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on large UPI payments, due after Diwali, would be the first fee on a bulk of these payments, and it would arrive just ahead of the listing window.

How much reaches Razorpay’s bottom line depends on two things: how it negotiates with the banks that receive the fee and the large merchants that pay the MDR.

Sources we spoke to suggest that much of the revenue bump that companies like Razorpay will get out of MDR would not boost their topline significantly, but could feed profits strongly because it is a fee on rails that companies have already built. For Razorpay, it’s a boost to its search for the right valuation just in time.

MDR on UPI would likely narrow the gap between the company’s sought valuation and its bottomline. It also gives Razorpay a growth story to take to public investors as it heads into the IPO.

A Profitable Core

Unlike many of its contemporaries eyeing a listing at the scale of Razorpay, the fintech has no major debt overhang and nearly half of the IPO proceeds are expected to be allocated for OFS.

Company sources told us that the core online payments business is EBITDA profitable and generating strong cash flows, which is why the company is making bold investments in allied businesses and AI.

Sources pointed towards capital allocations “between mature, cash-generating units and high-potential growth bets”, with AI-first products, financial infrastructure and new verticals taking the investment.

The company has also given a timeline on profitability. “By the end of FY26, our India business should be solidly profitable. At the consolidated level, we’ll reach profitability about two to three quarters after that,” the company’s CFO, Arpit Chug, told Inc42 in October 2025. 

But FY26 has since closed, and Razorpay is yet to make those numbers public. The biggest factor in Razorpay’s IPO will be the profitability and the margins earned by its core business. 

In lieu of actual profit figures, Razorpay’s pitch to public investors rests on scale. It described itself in 2024 as India’s market leader in digital payments processing, with a majority share, and said in 2025 that it served 105 of India’s 119 unicorns. It claims to be processing a total payments volume (TPV) of over $180 Bn (as of 2024 end). 

When compared against its primary competitors Cashfree and PayU, Razorpay stands out for its scale and its focus on small and medium businesses. 

Razorpay claims to lead on overall volumes, enterprise accounts drive the bulk of volumes at Cashfree, Inc42 reported earlier. Razorpay, on the other hand, claims that 80% of its client base comprises SMBs and startups.

Among the three, PayU India leads in terms of the topline. Its payments business alone earned $523 Mn (about ₹4,420 Cr) in FY25. It pulled ahead of Razorpay which reported ₹3,783 Cr in FY25, while Cashfree stood at ₹640.1 Cr. PayU owner Prosus claims the company has a 25% share of the Indian online payments, while processing $90 Bn in TPV in FY26.

In a bid to race past the competition, Razorpay has been eyeing overseas markets by strategic tie-ups and acquisitions. Mathur earlier said that international was its fastest-growing business, with payments growing about 40% and newer segments at 70-90%.

Outside India, Razorpay currently operates in Malaysia and Singapore and is eyeing expansion into the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam as its next Southeast Asian targets.

The company, according to sources, is expanding majorly within Southeast Asia and expects the revenue from these countries to contribute 15% of its overall topline by 2030.

Razorpay entered Malaysia by buying a majority stake in Curlec in 2022, launched its gateway there in 2023 and entered Singapore in March 2025.

Closer to home, the biggest expected lever is UPI and the introduction of MDR soon after the festive season. About half of the payments flowing through Razorpay are on UPI, and that rail is about to start earning the fee that can feed the company’s bottomline.

The Two Negotiations Behind Razorpay’s MDR Upside

The first critical negotiation for Razorpay will be with banks. Payment aggregators such as Razorpay get no fixed share under NPCI’s stated framework, because they are not direct members of the UPI network and are part of it only through sponsor banks.

So the aggregator’s cut has to come out of the acquirer bank’s share in the MDR, under a private contract between the two.

Reports suggest that the talks have centred on aggregators keeping 50-80% of the acquiring bank’s MDR share. But there is also a flip side to it.

Payment aggregators and gateways already earn technology, checkout and reconciliation fees from merchants, and with MDR coming into effect, the merchants can move to the aggregators and gateways that offer more reasonable take rates.

Pine Labs CEO Amrish Rau has already flagged that talks with merchants have yielded this view among the primary customer base for payments aggregators. “From a commercial standpoint, I absolutely do believe when it comes to the largest of large merchants that we have with us, there will be a commercial conversation to be had, for sure,” Rau said in October 2026 after the Q2 results.

Notwithstanding the restructured commercial agreements that the payment aggregators and gateways will sign with banks and merchants for the MDR regime, sources say that the fee could support higher valuations for IPO-bound companies such as Razorpay and PhonePe.

“The headline MDR pool is not the same as revenue accruing to an individual participant. It depends on eligible transaction volumes, merchant mix and the prescribed distribution across the ecosystem,” PhiCommerce CEO Rajesh Londhe told Inc42.

Listed peer Paytm has already put a number on what MDR will bring to the table. With its Q2 results, Paytm said it expects an uplift of about 2.5 bps in its overall payments processing margin, and that the actual outcome may stabilise in 2-3 quarters after implementation.

As per sources, MDR could bring Razorpay ₹192-461 Cr of revenue a year once implemented, which would be about 5-12% of its FY25 revenue and 15-36% of its FY25 gross profit.

As a result, analysts believe that Razorpay could see a valuation bump of $300 Mn-$1 Bn from the existing ask. That’s what the MDR effect can actually unlock, though much would also depend on the commercial agreements with banks and merchant talks.

Razorpay’s technology prowess and merchant scale could be a huge lever in any talks with banks and merchants.

However, what matters more than the scale will be the value of transactions and the scale of the clients themselves, which would directly boost revenue and improve margins. Nearly 80% of Razorpay’s customers are small businesses, digital-first brands and startups, and it has not disclosed how many of their tickets cross the ₹2,000 threshold required for the MDR boost.

There is also no certainty as yet on the timeline by which fintech companies can expect the MDR outcome to start showing up on their P&L.

Analysts tracking the industry, however, say that the companies would need a few quarters of data to give investors a credible outlook. For Paytm, that could be 2-3 quarters, and with Razorpay coming to the IPO table, investors would want to hear a number for the company. Will a listing between January and March of 2027 be enough to give investors a clear answer? 

The AI Story Needs Numbers

Then there’s the AI story, which we had written about extensively earlier this year.  

According to Mathur, Razorpay is building a long-term business bet on AI and this is not related to the  IPO and its outcome. The fintech sector has been one of the earliest adopters and partners of frontier AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude, experimenting with AI use cases for the millions of merchants on its platform.

 

Razorpay’s Agent Studio, built on Anthropic’s Claude, offers small businesses task-specific agents for abandoned carts, disputes, subscription recovery and cash flow forecasting. Mathur wants Razorpay to be known as “an operating system for businesses” which is run on AI. 

That story gives investors a reason to look past the thin margins in the payments business, but the AI theme is not strong enough in the case of Razorpay yet. It has to make a bigger splash in terms of the outcomes it is seeing. .

Rivals Cashfree, PayU and Pine Labs are also accelerating their AI led partnerships to offer new products to their existing merchant base. All these AI offerings have been particularly concentrated towards agentic workflows and ecommerce enablement. 

However, there is still little public evidence of what these agents earn. Mathur earlier told us that it will take a few years to assess the real term monetisation value that these AI capabilities can unlock for any fintech.

Hence for an IPO-bound Razorpay, its core payments business is the only true and measurable metric for the public investors. The future bets may fructify but for now, they are unlikely to be a factor for investors.

Even at a reported $5 Bn valuation, Razorpay goes to market with some real strengths such as 65% YoY revenue growth in FY25, about $180 Bn in annualised TPV, and a profitable core. While it is banking on the MDR regime to solve a lot of headaches, investors will want to see a lot more to justify the valuation ask. 

Whether the price holds depends on disclosures still to come, including its FY26 and subsequent financial performance and the results of its MDR negotiations with banks. And only then will Razorpay find out how much of its story the public market is willing to pay for.

[Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam]

The post MDR And AI: Inside The Two Acronyms That Could Shape Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO appeared first on Inc42 Media.

item.title: Mamaearth Parent Honasa’s Q2 Profit Jumps 87% YoY To ₹73 Cr
item.dc:creator: Vinaykumar Rai
item.description: Mamaearth parent Honasa Consumer reported an 86.7% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹73.2 Cr in the September quarter…
item.content:encoded:
Mamaearth parent Honasa Consumer reported an 86.7% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹73.2 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹39.2 Cr in the year-ago period.

The beauty and personal care (BPC) company’s operating revenue rose 35.9% to ₹731.2 Cr from ₹538.1 Cr in Q2 FY26.

“We delivered our highest growth since listing, with revenue growing 36% YoY and EBITDA nearly doubling to ₹93 Cr. What makes this growth particularly encouraging is the strength of the business behind it. Our focus categories grew over 40% and now contribute more than 80% of our business, with strong momentum across general trade, modern trade and ecommerce,” company’s cofounder and CEO Varun Alagh said. 

Sequentially, net profit declined 19% from ₹90.4 Cr, while operating revenue fell 3.3% from ₹755.9 Cr.

Honasa’s profit growth outpaced revenue growth on an annual basis, with total expenses increasing at a slower pace than its top line. The company’s expenses during the quarter surged 29.1% to ₹652.4 Cr from ₹505.5 Cr. The company’s tax expenses for the quarter more than doubled YoY to ₹27.6 Cr.

For the first half of the fiscal year, the Mamaearth parent reported an 31% YoY uptick in its top line to ₹1,487.1 Cr. Meanwhile, the company’s profit more than doubled YoY to ₹163.7 Cr.

Honasa’s Operational Updates

The BPC major said that its focus categories grew by 40%, taking their contribution to 80% of the company’s total income. The company estimates its shareholding in categories like face cleansers, shampoos, face serums, sunscreens, among others, to be about 5% in a market worth about ₹50,000 Cr. 

In terms of channel growth, Honasa claims to have achieved a 40% YoY growth in general trade secondary sales and modern trade offtake as well as a 20% growth in ecommerce. The company’s general trade presence expanded to about 3.2 Lakh outlets across India,

Beyond Mamaearth, Honasa’s ‘house of brands’ strategy sees it operate The Derma Co, Aqualogica, Staze, Dr Sheth’s, BBlunt, among others. In this, the company says that younger brands grew 45%+ during the quarter, with each brand building on its own growth drivers. 

The company doesn’t disclose particulars of the financial performance of its brands. For Mamaearth, Honasa said that it continued on its high-teens growth trajectory with mid-teens EBITDA.

Shares of Honasa were trading 4.02% lower at  ₹462.30 apiece on the BSE at 15:21 IST.

item.title: X Says Delhi Police Takedown Notices Against IFF, SFLC Were Fake
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against…
item.content:encoded:
Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC.in) were fake.

According to a post by IFF today, X said an internal investigation found the purported police communications to be fake and that it had filed a complaint with law enforcement authorities. X’s counsel told the court that an imposter had submitted the requests in the Delhi Police’s name.

“X stated that it is not likely to take any action at this stage,” IFF’s post added.

The court recorded X’s statement and disposed of the organisations’ petitions, granting them liberty to approach it again if the platform takes action against their accounts.

Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing both organisations, placed X’s transparency reports and a legal notice purportedly sent on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) on record.

IFF said it had written to the RSS seeking confirmation of the legal notice’s authenticity but received no response. Separately, SFLC.in said an email seeking verification of the takedown requests had bounced back from the Delhi Police address mentioned in the communication.

How The Dispute Began

IFF said X forwarded two ‘Illegal Content Reports’ to it on Tuesday (November 3), submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police.

The first, dated October 31, sought the removal of a post IFF published on October 30 and another by SFLC.in. The second, dated Monday (November 2), sought the removal of 37 posts and the withholding of the accounts of IFF, SFLC.in, and GeoBlockedIndia.

The reports alleged that the posts defamed the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The posts reproduced and commented on a legal notice the organisations said they had received in the RSS’s name.

IFF contested the requests, arguing that its posts were protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. It also questioned their legal basis, saying the reports cited no complaint, FIR, Magistrate’s order, or court order.

Through its counsel, IFF subsequently served a legal notice to the Delhi Police, with a copy to X, seeking withdrawal of the reports and details of the authority under which they had been submitted. It also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication.

IFF approached the Delhi High Court after receiving no official withdrawal or clarification from the Delhi Police.

Platform Accountability Under Scrutiny

The dispute comes amid a wider debate over content takedowns, transparency, and platforms’ responsibilities when responding to government requests.

In July, former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey claimed that the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove three URLs linked to bitchat, an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer communication without internet connectivity or centralised servers.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre’s (I4C) reported directive gave GitHub three hours to remove or disable access to the URLs. These covered the project’s main source code repository, Android repository, and Android releases page. The agency cited concerns over anonymous communication and difficulties in lawful interception and investigations.

Meanwhile, MeitY is reportedly exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000, from social media platforms. The provision limits intermediaries’ liability for third-party content, subject to prescribed conditions.

item.title: TRAI Backs Direct-To-Device Satellite Connectivity, Proposes New Authorisation Framework
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services…
item.content:encoded:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum.

The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage.

Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation.

The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services.

What Changes For Operators?

The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships.

For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation.

In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage.

However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation.

The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years.

Connecting Phones To Satellites

TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators.

For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India.

For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity.

However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use.

TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them.

TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee.

Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator.

Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz.

For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue.

The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

item.title: Cashfree Launches ‘Checkout For Agents’ To Enable AI-Led Payments
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Fintech soonicorn Cashfree Payments has launched ‘Checkout for Agents’, a new tool that enables AI agents to process customer payments…
item.content:encoded:
Fintech soonicorn Cashfree Payments has launched ‘Checkout for Agents’, a new tool that enables AI agents to process customer payments seamlessly. 

The new feature is built on the open-source WebMCP (model context protocol). The startup claims that merchants using Cashfree’s checkout page can avail the service without requiring any code changes or technical updates. 

The new solution aims to address a critical friction point in agentic commerce. While global purchases initiated by AI agents are projected to hit $1.5 Tn by 2030, traditional web interfaces remain optimised for human navigation. Hence, AI agents consume nearly 2 Mn tokens on average to decode the web page when they need to execute a transaction. 

By leveraging WebMCP, Cashfree claims that its new checkout tool directly communicates all the available actions to the AI agents, including reading order total and selecting payment mode. The startup claims its solution reduces token consumption by over 40%.

The architecture also allows personal AI assistants like Instinct, Meta’s Muse, and Grok Bot to reach the final payment step with fewer errors and lower drop-off rates, while leaving the final transaction authorisation with the user. 

“If an agent is visiting and browsing the merchant’s website, there will not be any drop off at the payment layer. Your speed of conversion will increase, token usage will drop, and the success rate will be near 100% as far as an agent making a payment is concerned,” Cashfree cofounder Reeju Datta told Inc42. 

He foresees AI agents driving a significant share of traffic to Cashfree’s customers in the future. “Agent traffic has grown around 4-5X annually and converts 5X better than my SEO traffic. The lifetime value (LTV) of such users is also much much higher,” Datta added.

On a question about AI agents taking unauthorised or unintended actions, Datta claimed that Cashfree’s latest offering preserves existing authorisation mechanisms and creates no heightened vulnerabilities. For instance, if the final payment authorisation step requires an OTP, then the user would still have to enter the pin to approve the payment. 

Founded in 2015 by Datta and Akash Sinha, Cashfree Payments offers digital payment solutions such as payment gateway, cross-border payments, payout solutions and banking APIs. It claims to process over $80 Bn in annual transaction volumes for over 10 Lakh businesses, including the likes of MakeMyTrip, Zomato, CRED, and Delhivery. 

Cashfree isn’t the only one in India’s startup ecosystem betting on agentic commerce. Its IPO-bound rival Razorpay is also repositioning itself as an AI-powered business operating system through its Agent Studio and agentic commerce push.

Then, there is Bengaluru-based Nudge that helps ecommerce brands optimise product discovery and conversions inside AI platforms. Foodtech giant Swiggy is also enabling users to interact with its app through external AI agents to discover food, build carts, place orders, and book restaurant tables.

item.title: CEO Harsh Jain Teases A Revamped Dream11 By 2026-End
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Erstwhile real money gaming (RMG) giant Dream11’s cofounder and CEO Harsh Jain has hinted at plans to launch a revamped…
item.content:encoded:
Erstwhile real money gaming (RMG) giant Dream11’s cofounder and CEO Harsh Jain has hinted at plans to launch a revamped version of the platform by 2026-end.

In a post on social media platform X, Jain said that the “brand new Dream11” would be built by sports fans and for sports fans. He did not disclose the upcoming platform’s features, commercial model or a specific launch date.

“A brand new Dream11 is launching (at the) end of Dec – by sports fans, for sports fans. Stay tuned…,” said Jain in his post.

The move signals Dream11’s next phase of evolution after the ban on online real-money gaming last year disrupted the platform’s paid fantasy sports business. While the teaser points to a product overhaul, it remains unclear how substantially the new offering will differ from its existing services. 

This comes more than a year after the Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Bill, 2025, which prohibited online real money games and restricted their promotion and advertising.

Following the legislation, Dream11 discontinued paid contests and pivoted to a watch-along platform where users can follow gameplays of prominent content creators. It has also been exploring alternative ways to engage sports fans. 

Last year, parent Dream Sports forayed into the wealth tech space under Dream Money and began offering mutual funds, digital gold, fixed deposits, and loans. It later also forayed into stockbroking with DreamStreet and forayed into the SaaS space with Dream Horizon.

However, it has been rethinking many of its newer bets. The startup shut down Dream Money in June this year. Dream Sports also quietly shut FanCode’s sports merchandise business earlier this year amid persistent issues with commercial viability. It also shut down its AI-powered sports performance analytics app Dream Play in June this year.

Nevertheless, the startup’s portfolio still remains substantial. FanCode continues to operate as a sports streaming platform, while DreamCricket represents its push into AAA gaming. It also has its investment platform DreamStreet.

Beyond the business challenges, Dream Sports is also facing GST dues of more than ₹20,000 Cr. In a blow to the company, the Supreme Court (SC), earlier this year, also upheld the tax authorities’ move to impose a 28% retrospective GST on real money online gaming companies over the full face value of bets placed through their platforms.

item.title: This Is Not About Money: Deepinder Goyal Defends Temple Amid Credibility Row
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Addressing social media debates over the scientific validity of Temple’s eponymous brain-monitoring wearable, founder Deepinder Goyal issued a statement directed…
item.content:encoded:
Addressing social media debates over the scientific validity of Temple’s eponymous brain-monitoring wearable, founder Deepinder Goyal issued a statement directed at “Concerned Indian Doctors”, asserting confidence in the R&D behind the wearables.

Goyal pointed out that Temple had already spent $30 Mn on its development, including $20 Mn of his personal money. He also noted that the company is raising funding from its employees and customers. 

“Selling a few thousand devices recovers a small fraction of this investment. A scam that pays nothing is not a scam anyone would run,”  the CEO wrote in his post. 

Goyal further said the product’s 14-day no-questions-asked return policy would validate its product in the market. 

On questions over Temple’s credibility and scientific validation, he argued that many wearable makers initially relied on internal studies before publishing external validation. He said the company would release pre-prints before peer-reviewed publications and it expects independent studies to emerge once the device becomes available more widely. 

In a follow-up post, Goyal also said, “Temple is a fitness tracker, and wellness device. We are not a medical device,” adding that the device hasn’t been clinically validated. 

Important to highlight that pre-orders for the wearable officially opened on November 1, with a hefty listing price of ₹85,000.  Units are hand-made to order and expected to begin shipping roughly three months after purchase, starting in early 2027.

What Doctors Say About Temple?

For context, several medical experts had criticised Temple over its claim that a wearable sensor placed near the temple can reliably measure cerebral blood flow. 

Hepatologist Dr Cyriac Abby Philips, popularly known as The Liver Doc, published an Instagram carousel calling the product “the biggest health scam and wellness fraud in India,” saying the device can only detect when blood rushes to one’s face. 

Gurugram-based gastroenterologist Dr Zubin Sharma also noted that blood flows to the brain via arteries in the neck and back of head, not the temple. 

Additionally, many on social media pointed out that studies published on Temple’s website were not peer-reviewed, and were funded and conducted by the company itself. They also raised questions about the validity of Goyal’s Gravity Ageing Hypothesis, which links the long-term effects of gravity on blood circulation to ageing. 

In fact, Dr Philips doubled down on the criticism of Temple in a reply to Goyal’s latest post, calling out Temple’s claims of reading blood flow to the brain and the company’s explanation of its proprietary ‘Entropy’ score.

The Temple Journey So Far

Goyal’s move into brain-monitoring wearables has been taking shape through a series of bets on longevity research. This began with his personal research initiative Continue Research, which he referred to as his personal health and wellness venture back in 2024.

The initiative remained largely under wraps for over a year before unveiling its first hypothesis, Gravity Ageing, in November 2025. The hypothesis proposed that gravity’s effect on cerebral blood flow (CBF) could be an overlooked contributor to human ageing.

Temple emerged around the same time as a commercial extension of this research. Inc42 first reported in November 2025 that Goyal was exploring a wearable device company focused on health monitoring. The device, which he had been seen wearing near his temple, was being used experimentally to measure blood flow to the brain in real time.

“I left the Eternal CEO role to chase purpose with Temple. This is not about money. I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck,” Goyal said. 

On the product front, Temple has been developing a wearable that sits on the forehead near the temple and tracks signals associated with cerebral blood flow. Goyal revealed a smaller version of the device in August, claiming it was less than half the size of its earlier iteration. It has worked with contract manufacturers Zetwerk and Ethereal Machines to scale production, while retaining some manufacturing capabilities in-house. 

The startup began taking shape as a standalone venture earlier this year. In February, Temple raised $54 Mn (around ₹493 Cr) in a seed funding round at a post-money valuation of approximately $190 Mn. The round was led by Goyal, who invested a little over ₹100 Cr, with participation from Steadview Capital, Peak XV Partners, Vy Capital, Info Edge Ventures, among others. More than 30 employees also participated in the round. 

Temple subsequently expanded its ambitions beyond hardware. In July 2026, it acquired London-based longevity medicine practice Longevous for an undisclosed amount, bringing clinical and scientific expertise into the business.

item.title: Go Digit Q2 Profit Falls 31% To ₹142 Cr
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Insurtech Go Digit reported a 31.1% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to…
item.content:encoded:
Insurtech Go Digit reported a 31.1% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to ₹142.4 Cr from ₹206.8 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. The insurtech major’s profit also declined 62.4% sequentially from ₹378.61 Cr in the June quarter.

The decline in profitability came despite a marginal increase in insurance revenue, which rose 1.7%  to ₹2,720.5 Cr during the quarter from ₹2,674.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, insurance revenue increased 2.1% from ₹2,665.6 Cr.

Segment-wise, Motor Third Party (TP) insurance remained Go Digit’s largest business, contributing ₹1,066.1 Cr to insurance revenue in Q2 FY27, up 8.3% YoY. Motor Own Damage (OD) insurance revenue grew at a faster pace of 11.4% YoY to ₹640.64 Cr.

The company’s gross written premium for the quarter dipped by 3.6% YoY to ₹2,571 Cr while gross direct premium, dipped 1.2% to ₹2,351 Cr.

However, the company’s insurance service result, which reflects the profitability of its insurance operations before investment and other financial income, sunk 73.4% YoY to ₹43 Cr from ₹161.98 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The figure also fell 62.3% sequentially from ₹114 Cr.

The deterioration in the insurance service result came as insurance service expenses increased 22.4% YoY to ₹2,607.73 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹2,130.85 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Incurred claims rose 9.2% to ₹1,968.03 Cr from ₹1,802.96 Cr, while employee benefit expenses increased 4.3% to ₹95.48 Cr.

Commission expenses, on the other hand, declined 2.6% YoY to ₹781.88 Cr from ₹803.10 Cr. Other insurance service expenses increased 1.7% to ₹94.52 Cr.

On the investment front, Go Digit reported a 20.6% YoY increase in investment income to ₹368.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹305.5 Cr in the year-ago period. However, investment income declined 39.2% sequentially from ₹606.47 Cr.

The company’s net finance result, which includes investment income and insurance finance income or expenses, increased 28.6% YoY to ₹196.94 Cr.

Consequently, Go Digit’s profit before tax (PBT) declined 31.2% YoY to ₹190.18 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹276.30 Cr in Q2 FY26. The figure was also down 62.4% sequentially from ₹505.96 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Total tax expense stood at ₹47.79 Cr during the quarter, comprising current tax of ₹3.93 Cr and deferred tax of ₹43.86 Cr. This compared with a total tax expense of ₹69.51 Cr in Q2 FY26.

For the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), Go Digit reported a 3.2% YoY decline in net profit to ₹521 Cr from ₹538.23 Cr in H1 FY26. Insurance revenue increased 4.5% YoY to ₹5,386.09 Cr during the six-month period.

Shares of Go Digit ended today’s trading session 1.05% higher at ₹260.30.

item.title: Venomics AI Raises $2.7 Mn To Turn Venom Into Medicine
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio.

The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads.

The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to expand its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery, while supporting the validation and optimisation of promising molecules.

Founded in 2026 by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, Venomics AI is working to tap the largely unexplored molecular diversity found in animal venoms to identify potential drug candidates.

Animal venoms contain complex molecules that have evolved over millions of years to interact with specific biological targets. Some of these compounds have already inspired medicines.

However, a large part of the molecular diversity across venomous species remains unexplored, presenting an opportunity for drug discovery.

Venomics AI is building a platform that combines molecular sequencing and venom biology to map this diversity through its Venom Atlas. It then uses AI to prioritise promising molecular candidates and validates its predictions through functional laboratory screening.

“Animal venoms represent one of nature’s richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and at Venomics AI, we are combining cutting-edge experimental science with artificial intelligence to unlock this extraordinary potential,” Sunagar said.

India’s bioeconomy is on track to reach $300 Bn by 2030, with the country’s rapid emergence as a global biotechnology hub, based on IBEF data. Notably, the biotech sector in the country has been booming in recent years. The country is home to more than 11,000 biotech startups.

Also, as part of the Budget 2027, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a new ‘Biopharma SHAKTI’ scheme with an outlay of ₹10,000 Cr.

Meanwhile, investor interest in this space has been gradually seeing an uptick, where earlier this year, Cellogen Therapeutics secured ₹20 Cr in funding from Kotak Alternate Asset Managers (Kotak Alts), while StrainX Bioworks has raised $13 Mn in a funding round led by Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital.

item.title: SaaS Company RateGain’s Q2 Profit Rises 47% YoY To ₹75 Cr
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Travel-focused SaaS company RateGain reported a 46.5% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in the September quarter…
item.content:encoded:
Travel-focused SaaS company RateGain reported a 46.5% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹51 Cr a year ago.

Operating revenue jumped 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn in November last year.

Sequentially, net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr, while operating revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr.

RateGain reported negative other income of ₹26.2 Lakh, taking its total income to ₹745.1 Cr. Total expenses rose about 158% YoY to ₹647.7 Cr.

Adjusted for deferred deal consideration related to the Sojern acquisition, RateGain said its net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr.

For H1 FY27, operating revenue increased 169.5% YoY to ₹1,530.4 Cr from ₹568 Cr. Reported EBITDA rose 214.2% to ₹324.5 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA increased 250.9% to ₹362.5 Cr.

The company said its reported H1 EBITDA had already exceeded its full-year FY26 EBITDA.

Sojern Integration And Debt

The Sojern acquisition expanded RateGain’s travel marketing business, particularly its presence among destination marketing organisations (DMOs), hotels, and other travel businesses.

To finance the acquisition, RateGain’s UK subsidiary secured a $125 Mn debt facility from HSBC and Citibank, backed by a corporate guarantee from the Indian parent.

Including a repayment of $46.3 Mn today, the subsidiary has repaid $93.8 Mn, or 75%, of the original facility. Its outstanding debt now stands at $31.3 Mn.

Alongside the expansion in revenue, RateGain said the Sojern integration helped broaden its customer base. It had 14,538 customers at the end of September, about 4.5X the 3,224 customers it had at the end of FY25.

Its customers include hospitality companies, online travel agencies (OTAs), airlines, car rental companies, and DMOs.

Marketing Drives Business Mix

RateGain operates across three verticals: data as a service (DaaS), distribution, and marketing technology. Its offerings span competitive pricing and demand intelligence, hotel distribution, digital marketing, and guest engagement.

Marketing technology now accounts for 80.2% of revenue, followed by DaaS at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%.

By customer industry, hospitality contributed 48.6% of H1 revenue, followed by DMOs at 30.9%, OTAs at 7.2%, airlines at 3.7%, and car rentals at 2.3%.

North America accounted for 63.7% of H1 revenue, followed by Europe at 21.5%, Asia-Pacific at 12.3%, and other markets at 2.5%.

The company’s client roster includes 33 of the world’s top 40 hotel chains, four of the top five airlines, and seven of the top 10 car rental companies.

RateGain also highlighted its AI products. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said shifting travel demand is increasing customers’ reliance on data and AI.

He said RateGain’s priorities included adding customers, increasing their use of its platform, and extending AI into more of their daily operations. In H2 FY27, the company plans to take the combined RateGain and Sojern offering to more customers.

RateGain reported a total pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr.

The company’s employee headcount stood at 1,244 at the end of September, up 42.8% YoY.

Shares of RateGain ended today’s trading session 3.3% higher at ₹819.50 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: [Update] Exclusive: RapidClaims In Talks To Raise $30 Mn
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Update | November 5, 19:43 After the story was published, RapidClaims founder and CEO Dushyant Mishra said the startup is…
item.content:encoded:
Update | November 5, 19:43

After the story was published, RapidClaims founder and CEO Dushyant Mishra said the startup is not in talks with WestBridge Capital to raise any funding round. He also said that the $200 Mn valuation figure is “incorrect”.

Original | October 5, 18:22

AI-powered SaaS startup RapidClaims is in talks to raise around $30 Mn in a funding round led by WestBridge Capital at a valuation of about $200 Mn, sources told Inc42.

The round is expected to be its Series B, with existing investors Accel and Together Fund likely to participate, the sources added.

RapidClaims did not respond to questions sent by Inc42, while WestBridge Capital declined to comment. 

Founded in 2023 by Dushyant Mishra, Abhinay Vyas, and Jot Sarup Singh, RapidClaims builds AI-powered revenue cycle management (RCM) software that helps healthcare providers automate medical coding, improve clinical documentation, prevent insurance claim denials, and recover outstanding payments.

The startup primarily caters to healthcare providers in the US, helping them address billing errors, rejected claims, and delays in reimbursements.

Automating Healthcare Revenue Workflows

RapidClaims’ products include RapidCode for medical coding, RapidVBC for clinical documentation and risk adjustment, and RapidRecovery for managing denied claims, automating appeals, and detecting underpayments.

The platform integrates with healthcare providers’ existing electronic health record systems. It serves physician groups, hospitals, health systems, federally qualified health centres (FQHCs), and ambulatory surgery centres, among other healthcare organisations.

The startup is also developing inpatient coding capabilities with design partners, extending its automation tools to coding for hospital admissions.

In April 2025, RapidClaims raised $8 Mn in a Series A round led by Accel, with participation from Together Fund. It also disclosed that it had previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding. RapidClaims had earmarked the Series A proceeds for expanding its go-to-market efforts, strengthening its technology and product capabilities, and growing its sales and marketing teams. 

At the time, the startup said it had grown sixfold over the preceding four months and served a double-digit client base. It was also looking to expand its presence among FQHCs, physician groups, outpatient facilities, and ambulatory surgery centres. 

Investors Bet On Automation

The proposed fundraise comes amid increasing investor interest in startups looking to automate healthcare administration and insurance workflows.

In October, Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in a Series A extension led by Z47, taking its total Series A funding to $22.5 Mn. The startup develops AI agents for tasks including appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills, and payment collection.

Meanwhile, Consint.AI raised ₹22 Cr to expand internationally and develop its AI capabilities for fraud detection and claims processing. Its products automate claims processing, digitise documents, and standardise healthcare records.
